lessons.title: Cleaning materials and how to use them
lessons.html:
Why cleanliness matters in the dairy

Milk is a perfect food for people, and also for germs. Germs from dirty teats, hands, equipment or water get into milk and multiply quickly. Dirty milk sours fast, is paid a lower price by the buyer, and can make people sick. A clean dairy gives safe milk and better prices.

Types of cleaning materials

MaterialWhat it does
Alkaline detergentRemoves milk fat and protein from equipment
Acid cleanerRemoves milkstone (hard white mineral layer) from pipes and the bulk tank
Sanitiser (for example chlorine-based or iodine-based)Kills germs left after cleaning
Teat dip or sprayKills germs on teats after milking

Mixing cleaning materials

  1. Read the label. It gives the mixing strength and water temperature.
  2. Wear gloves, goggles and an apron.
  3. Measure the water first, then add the measured chemical to the water.
  4. Use the correct measuring jug, kept only for that chemical.
  5. Never mix two chemicals together. Chlorine and acid together make a poisonous gas.
  6. Keep chemicals in their labelled containers, locked away from milk and from children.

Too weak a mix does not clean. Too strong a mix wastes money, damages rubber parts and can leave residues in milk. Measure every time.

First aid

Chemical in the eyes: rinse with lots of clean running water and get help. Chemical on the skin: wash with plenty of water. First aid must be learned in hands-on training by an accredited provider.

lessons.title: Milking methods and hygiene during milking
lessons.html:
Milking methods

  • Hand milking: used on small farms. The milker squeezes the teat between the thumb and fingers from the top down, into a clean bucket.
  • Bucket milking machine: a portable machine milks into a closed bucket.
  • Pipeline or parlour milking: cows come into a milking parlour (for example a herringbone or rotary parlour); milk flows through pipes straight to the bulk tank.

Milking routine

  1. Bring cows in calmly. Stressed cows let down less milk.
  2. Wash and dry your hands, or wear clean gloves.
  3. Fore-strip a few squirts from each teat into a strip cup. Look for clots, flakes, blood or watery milk: these are signs of mastitis.
  4. Clean the teats: pre-dip or wash, then dry each cow with its own paper towel or cloth. Never put clusters on wet, dirty teats.
  5. Attach the cluster (or start hand milking) soon after preparing, while the milk lets down.
  6. Remove the cluster when the milk stops flowing. Over-milking damages teats.
  7. Post-dip all teats with teat dip to kill germs.

Rules

  • Milk cows with mastitis, or cows under antibiotic treatment, last, and keep their milk out of the bulk tank. Follow the withdrawal period on the product label or from your vet.
  • Mark treated cows clearly, for example with leg bands.
  • Keep the parlour floor clean during milking.

lessons.title: Rapid cooling and milk quality
lessons.html:
Why cool milk quickly

Milk comes out of the cow at body temperature. That warmth is ideal for germs, which can double in number in a short time. Cooling milk quickly in the bulk tank slows germ growth, keeps milk fresh and keeps the bacterial count low. Milk buyers test the milk and pay less, or reject it, if counts are high.

  • Switch on the bulk tank cooling before or as soon as milk starts flowing in.
  • Check the tank thermometer and record the temperature as the farm procedure says.
  • Keep the tank lid closed.
  • Report a tank that is not cooling at once.

Assessing milk quality

On the farm

  • Look: clean milk is white or creamy, without clots, blood, flakes or dirt.
  • Smell: fresh milk smells clean. Sour or strange smells mean a problem.
  • Strip cup: checks each quarter for mastitis.
  • California Mastitis Test (CMT): a paddle and reagent show if a quarter has a high cell count; the mix becomes thick like jelly.
  • Filter sock or milk filter: check after milking for dirt and clots.

Laboratory tests by the buyer

  • Bacterial count (hygiene and cooling)
  • Somatic cell count (udder health)
  • Antibiotic residues
  • Added water, fat and protein

A bad result tells the farm what to fix: cleaning, cooling, milking routine or udder health.

lessons.title: Cleaning the milking equipment
lessons.html:
Clean after every milking

Milk left in pipes, clusters and buckets becomes a home for germs. Equipment must be cleaned after every milking.

Cleaning steps for a milking machine

  1. Pre-rinse with lukewarm water straight after milking to wash out milk. Do not use very hot water first, because it bakes milk protein onto surfaces. Do not re-circulate the rinse water.
  2. Hot detergent wash: circulate hot alkaline detergent at the strength and temperature on the label, for the time the label or equipment supplier says. The water must still be hot at the end.
  3. Rinse with clean water.
  4. Acid wash as often as the programme says, to remove milkstone.
  5. Sanitise before the next milking if your programme says so.
  6. Drain everything so no water stays in the system.

Bulk tank

  • Clean after every collection: rinse, wash with detergent, rinse, sanitise.
  • Clean the outlet valve and the lid.
  • Check for milkstone and milk residues.

Hand-milking buckets and cans

  • Rinse with cold or lukewarm water, scrub with detergent and a brush, rinse, sanitise, and turn upside down on a rack to dry.

Check rubber parts

Liners and tubes wear and crack. Cracks hold germs. Replace them as the supplier recommends.

Key points

  • Measure cleaning chemicals exactly and never mix two chemicals.
  • Fore-strip, clean and dry teats before milking, and post-dip after.
  • Keep milk from treated or mastitis cows out of the bulk tank.
  • Cool milk quickly to slow germ growth.
  • Rinse, hot-wash, rinse, acid-wash and sanitise equipment as the programme says.
